title: module-compatibility-matrix-upgrade-playbook-v2
body:
Purpose:
This is a working-draft compatibility matrix and upgrade playbook for the set of Terraform primitives we maintain for private deployments (VPC, IAM, cluster primitives for EKS/GKE/AKS). The goal: provide a prescriptive, reproducible path for bumping module versions, handling breaking changes across clouds, and minimizing customer downtime during upgrades.

Scope:
- VPC primitives: subnets (public/private), route tables, NAT gateways, endpoints
- IAM primitives: cross-account roles, service account mappings (IRSA/workload identity/managed identity)
- Cluster primitives: EKS/GKE/AKS cluster module surface (node pools, autoscaler, CNI, kubelet flags)
- Outputs/variables standardization and naming conventions
- Upgrade & rollback playbook for major/minor patches

High-level rules (must follow):
1) Semantic versioning on all modules (MAJOR = breaking API change, MINOR = new features compatible, PATCH = bugfix).
2) Always add backward-compatible outputs when introducing new features; avoid removing outputs until one major cycle.
3) Surface a "compatibility" boolean variable when a change could alter downstream resource names (default true = compatibility shim on).
4) Preserve state layout: avoid renaming resources in-place without a documented state-migration step.

Compatibility matrix (condensed text):
- VPC module v1.x (AWS/GCP/Azure):
  - AWS: supports explicit public and private subnets, NAT gateways, route tables, VPC endpoints (s3/ssm/ecr). Breaking changes: subnet name/tagging rename must be accompanied by state mv + resource replace plan.
  - GCP: supports shared VPC vibe, private service connect, route removal is sensitive; changing subnetwork ip_cidr requires recreate.
  - Azure: allow/deny NSG attachments vary by API version; keep NSG attachments as separate resources to reduce re-apply churn.
- IAM module v1.x:
  - AWS: recommended to expose role_arn and policy_arns. For IRSA support expose iam_openid_connect_provider and option to create OIDC.
  - GCP: expose service_account_email and iam_bindings outputs.
  - Azure: expose managed_identity_id and role_assignment_ids.
- Cluster modules (EKS/GKE/AKS) v2.x:
  - EKS: expected variables: cluster_name, node_groups (map), enable_irsa, cni (amazon-vpc-cni | calico | custom). Breaking changes: switching CNI default will require node replacement.
  - GKE: workload_identity vs static service accounts — module should expose workload_identity_pool and service_account_email outputs.
  - AKS: managed identity switching will replace cluster in-place in older API versions; document version gate.

Standard variable/output conventions (recommended):
- Variables (canonical names):
  - environment (string)
  - region (string)
  - azs (list)
  - vpc_cidr (string)
  - public_subnet_cidrs (list)
  - private_subnet_cidrs (list)
  - enable_private_endpoint (bool)
  - enable_irsa (bool)
  - node_pools (map) -> each pool: instance_types, min_size, max_size, taints, labels
  - kubelet_extra_args (string)
  - service_cidr (string)
  - pod_cidr (string)

- Outputs (canonical names):
  - vpc_id
  - vpc_cidr
  - public_subnet_ids
  - private_subnet_ids
  - route_table_ids
  - nat_gateway_ids
  - internet_gateway_id (AWS)
  - cluster_endpoint
  - cluster_certificate_authority_data
  - cluster_security_group_id (AWS)
  - cluster_oidc_provider_arn (AWS)
  - kubeconfig (string, base64 encoded)
  - node_role_arn

Example recommended variable block (to copy into modules):

variable "environment" {
  description = "deployment environment (prod/staging/dev)"
  type        = string
}

variable "node_pools" {
  description = "map of node-pool configs"
  type        = map(any)
  default     = {}
}

Example outputs (text):
output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id }
output "private_subnet_ids" { value = aws_subnet.private[*].id }

Upgrade playbook (step-by-step):
1) Pre-cut: create a branch with module bump and smoke test changes isolated in a sandbox account.
2) Release notes: document all new outputs, variable defaults, and explicit breaking changes. Publish to Confluence + internal slack channel #private-deployments.
3) Canary: pick a non-critical customer/private deployment to run through the full TF apply and integration tests. Validate network connectivity (DNS, S3/ECR access), node pool scaling, and control-plane endpoints.
4) State compatibility check: run terraform plan with the upgraded module and inspect any resource renames. If resource names changed, create a state migration script using 'terraform state mv' and test it.
5) Database/State backup: snapshot Terraform state (remote backend snapshot) and cloud provider resources (e.g., AMIs, snapshots for persistent data) where applicable.
6) Rollout: perform staged upgrades (1 region/account/cluster at a time). Wait at least two autoscaler cycles and validate metrics.
7) Post-upgrade validation: run integration tests, validate RBAC role bindings, check kube-system pods, and run a smoke harness that runs 100 native requests to customer endpoints.
8) Observability: ensure Console traces/metrics show no large latency spikes or 5xx spikes.
9) Rollback plan: if issues discovered, use the following sequence:
   - Revert Terraform module version in the branch and run terraform apply (unless resources were destroyed).
   - If resources were replaced, rollback must include state mv back to previous resource IDs or restore from state snapshot.
   - If control-plane broken, re-create kubeconfig from saved output and re-run node provisioning using previous AMI/node pool configs.

Cloud-specific upgrade notes (quick):
- AWS (EKS): IRSA on by default; when enabling IRSA for an existing cluster, watch for IAM role name collisions. When changing CNI versions, drain nodes in small batches. Beware of ENI limits on certain instance types (t3.medium not recommended for dense pods).
- GCP (GKE): pod IP range changes are disruptive; use alias IPs carefully. When enabling private cluster endpoints, ensure VPN/Cloud NAT is in place for control-plane egress.
- Azure (AKS): upgrading the cluster control-plane sometimes forces node pool recreation; schedule maintenance window and validate Azure API versions used by the module.

Known pitfalls and mitigations (field notes):
- "Subnet renames causing mass replacement": mitigation -> keep subnet resource names stable; add compatibility flag that creates new resources with explicit dependencies and then deprecate old outputs in next major.
- "State drift after manual edits": mitigation -> disallow critical infra changes outside Terraform for private deployments; add pre-apply checks that call provider APIs and compare diffs.
- "Cross-account role race during rollouts": mitigation -> pre-create roles in target accounts and reference by ARN; avoid on-the-fly role creation when many accounts update at once.

Testing matrix (minimum):
- unit: terraform validate + tflint + terrascan on modules
- integration: terratest (or kitchen-terraform) smoke to create/destroy in sandbox
- canary: run a full customer-like traffic replay on a canary cluster for 72 hours before broad rollout

Appendix: recommended git/terraform workflow
- Branch per major bump: module/v2 -> PR with changelog and upgrade notes
- Release tag: semver tag on module repo and changelog in releases.md
- Change control: major bumps require a short RFC doc and approval by eng-private-deployments and eng-sre.

Quick reference: actions to take when bumping a module major version:
- Draft RFC / Confluence change with migration steps (link to example)
- Publish module with v2.0.0 tag to registry (internal)
- Create 'migration' terraform plan showing intended state changes and state mv commands
- Schedule the rollout and canary testing

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add concrete state-migration examples for: subnet renames, iam role renames, node_pool resource id changes.
- Prepare automated 'preflight' script that does provider-side diff and warns of potential replacements.
- Write a quick utility to translate old terraform outputs to new output names to ease downstream module upgrades.

Unresolved questions:
- Do we want to introduce an explicit compatibility shim module that mirrors old output names for one major cycle? (pros/cons documented but not decided).
- Should we standardize on a single CNI default across customers or let module choices vary per deployment?

References and links (working list):
- Confluence: PD-ops-vpc-design (internal)
- Jira: PD-6789 (module versioning epic)
- GitHub PR: repo/terraform-modules/pr/314 (prototype of compatibility flag)

End of draft.
